forefront: Protection from outsiders is owed and overdue. Who protects the insider from the elder?
branches: They are thousands of distinct nations, languages, and lineages, and treating them as one category is itself a colonial artifact.
law: This entry refuses the general form of the question, because outside compulsion is the historical wound itself.
money: Money comes from ceremony fees, healing payments, initiation costs and offerings.
reach: The control risk is that the same secrecy can shield a specific abusive elder from community accountability.
techniques: Thirty named techniques from domestic-abuse and social-psychology research, applied to institutions, in the eight stages of the cycle.
loops: The seven loops below show how the practices connect, so that each step makes the next one easier and the last step feeds the first.
say-do: Apologies issued, individuals named, records still withheld and settlements still unmet.
ledger: Extractive research and cultural licensing have published, patented, and monetized knowledge without community consent or benefit-sharing.
who-gets-hurt: The table below sets out who carries the heaviest weight and what each harm compounds with.
tiers: The table lists four roles in communities and research, what each does, what each sees, what each is asked to do and what each could refuse.
precedent: The standing invitation to community reviewers takes precedence over every other editorial rule on it.
voices: The survivors who spoke to the TRC, whose testimony made the "cultural genocide" finding.
questions: Ask a non-Indigenous person selling your ceremony to name the community that authorized them.
leaving: Domestic violence support run by and for Native people is available in the US.
